q: How much of what you experience did you actually choose to notice?
w: The Principles of Psychology, ch. XI
g: Attention is the mind taking possession of one of several simultaneously possible objects. Experience is not given but selected: my experience is what I agree to attend to. What you call your personality is partly a settled pattern of what you notice and what you let pass.
p: For one hour, every time your attention moves, write one line: what pulled it, something outside or a thought of your own.

q: What is your mind doing when it leaves the room?
w: The Science of Mind Wandering, Annual Review of Psychology 66
g: Mind-wandering is not a lapse but a large share of waking thought: self-generated, often future-directed, only partly under control. The review separates deliberate from involuntary wandering, and the distinction matters. Deliberate wandering is where planning and writing happen. Involuntary wandering is where rumination lives.
p: Three alarms a day for three days. At each, label the last five minutes: on task, deliberately elsewhere, or hijacked.

q: Is an unhappy mind a wandering mind, or the reverse?
w: A Wandering Mind Is an Unhappy Mind, Science 330
g: Experience sampling from about 2,250 adults: people report mind-wandering in 46.9 per cent of sampled moments, and they are less happy when they do, including when the wandering is to pleasant topics. The temporal ordering suggests the wandering precedes the unhappiness rather than following it.
p: Compare your worst hours this week against your least demanding hours. If they coincide, the problem is not the work.

q: What subject does your brain return to when nothing else claims it?
w: A default mode of brain function, PNAS 98
g: A set of regions is more active at rest than during goal-directed tasks. The finding is often oversold as the brain's self, but the measured claim is narrower: there is a baseline mode, it is metabolically expensive, and it is suppressed when a task demands attention.
p: Sit for ten minutes with nothing to do and no phone. Note the first three topics your mind returns to. Those are your default mode's preferred objects.

q: When does attention stop feeling like effort?
w: Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience
g: Flow is reported when challenge slightly exceeds skill and feedback is immediate. The experience-sampling method behind it is sound; the construct is not. Flow is measured almost entirely by self-report at the moment of the report, so it cannot easily be separated from the enjoyment it is supposed to explain.
p: Log three tasks this week on two axes: challenge and skill. Look for the corner where both are high.

q: Do you know why you did that, or do you know a story about why you did that?
w: Telling More Than We Can Know, Psychological Review 84
g: People confidently report causes for their own behaviour that the experimental manipulations show cannot be the cause. The reports are not lies; they are confabulations produced after the fact. The limit is specific: we lack direct access to the processes that generate judgements, and we substitute a plausible theory.
p: Write the reason for your last three purchases or refusals. Then write what else changed in the hour before each. Note where the stated reason cannot carry the decision.

q: Which facts about you would someone else report more accurately?
w: Who Knows What About a Person? The Self-Other Knowledge Asymmetry, Perspectives on Psychological Science 5
g: The self-other knowledge asymmetry model: for traits that are evaluative and observable, other people predict behaviour better than you do. For traits that are internal and hard to observe, you are the better judge. Self-knowledge is not uniformly good or bad; it is good on some axes and systematically poor on others.
p: Pick one trait you are confident about. Ask two people who see you weekly to rate it 1-7 without explanation. Compare. Disagreement is data, not insult.

q: Why does your own bias look smaller from the inside?
w: Perception and Misperception of Bias in Human Judgment, Trends in Cognitive Sciences 11
g: We detect bias in others by their behaviour, and in ourselves by introspection. Introspection returns intentions, not processes, so our own biases stay invisible while theirs look obvious. The asymmetry is produced by the method, not by being less biased.
p: Name a judgement you made this week that went against you. Write the strongest case that it was biased. Then write why that case is wrong. If the second is easier, note that.

q: How clearly defined is your idea of yourself?
w: Self-Concept Clarity: Measurement, Personality Correlates, and Cultural Boundaries, JPSP 70
g: Self-concept clarity is the extent to which self-beliefs are clearly and confidently defined, internally consistent, and stable over time. It is measurable, it is distinct from self-esteem, and low clarity tracks with rumination and poorer wellbeing. Clarity is not the same as being right about yourself.
p: Write five statements beginning I am. Two weeks later, write five more without looking. Compare. Stability and contradiction are both information.

q: Is there an owner of your experience, or only a series of experiences?
g: Parfit argues that personal identity is not what matters: there is no further fact about a self that persists, only psychological continuity and connectedness. The argument is not empirical and does not claim to be. It matters here because many self-descriptions assume a single owner behind the reports, and that assumption is a philosophical choice, not a finding.
p: Describe yourself as you were ten years ago in five lines. Then describe the person who did those things in the third person. Note what survives the change of pronoun.

q: Can you tell one bad feeling from another?
w: Knowing What You're Feeling and Knowing What to Do About It, Cognition and Emotion 15
g: People differ in how finely they distinguish negative emotions. Higher differentiation predicts better regulation: a person who can separate anger from disappointment from fatigue can act on the specific one. A single label for everything negative leaves only one move.
p: Twice a day for a week, name the feeling with two words instead of one, and state what it is aimed at. If no second word comes, write none.

q: Where does a mood come from before you name it?
w: Interoceptive Inference, Emotion, and the Embodied Self, Trends in Cognitive Sciences 17
g: Emotion is modelled as inference about the causes of bodily signals rather than a readout of them. On this account a mood is a prediction about your internal state, and the prediction can be wrong. This is a framework with strong support for the mechanism and much weaker support for any specific therapeutic recipe built on it.
p: For three days, before naming a mood, note four bodily facts: sleep, food, movement, temperature. Name the mood after.

q: How long will this actually affect you?
w: Affective Forecasting, Advances in Experimental Social Psychology 35
g: People overestimate the intensity and duration of future emotional reactions, a bias driven partly by immune neglect: we underestimate the psychological systems that will blunt the impact. The systematic error runs in one direction, toward predicting that events matter longer than they do.
p: Write a prediction: how will you feel in two weeks about something happening now, 1-10. Set a reminder for two weeks and record the actual number.

q: Is it better to change the situation or to clamp the reaction?
w: Antecedent- and Response-Focused Emotion Regulation, JPSP 74
g: Reappraisal (changing the interpretation before the emotion runs) reduces negative affect and costs little. Suppression (inhibiting the expression after the emotion runs) reduces the visible expression while leaving or raising physiological arousal, and it impairs memory for the episode. The distinction is about timing, not virtue.
p: Take one recurring irritation this week. Write the appraisal you run. Then write one alternative appraisal that is also true.

q: Do you want the want you acted on?
w: Freedom of the Will and the Concept of a Person, Journal of Philosophy 68
g: What distinguishes a person is not reason but second-order desire: wanting to want something, or wanting not to. Freedom of the will is the alignment of the will acted on with the will one wants to have. Addiction is the case where the two come apart.
p: Pick one first-order desire active today. State your second-order stance on it. If there is a gap, that gap is where the problem lives.

q: Why does deciding to do it not make it happen?
w: Implementation Intentions and Goal Achievement: A Meta-Analysis, Advances in Experimental Social Psychology 38
g: Across 94 studies, if-then plans linking a specified cue to a specified response showed a medium-to-large effect on goal attainment, d around 0.65. The mechanism is cue delegation: the decision is made once, in advance, and the situation triggers it. Wanting it more is not the active ingredient; specifying when and where is.
p: Take one intention you have failed at twice. Rewrite it as: when X happens, I will do Y. Name the exact cue.

q: How much of your character is the room you are standing in?
g: Situationist social psychology found behaviour predicted better by immediate circumstances than by global traits: the same person is honest, cruel, or helpful depending on noise, hurry, and who else is present. The strong reading is that character traits as usually conceived do not exist; the weak reading is that they are far more situational than we report.
p: Take one I am the kind of person who claim. Find the situations where it fails. Then change the situations rather than the self-description.

q: Is willpower a fuel that runs out?
w: A Multilab Preregistered Replication of the Ego-Depletion Effect, Perspectives on Psychological Science 11
g: The ego-depletion literature rested on a large effect from small studies. A preregistered replication across 23 laboratories with over 2,000 participants found an effect indistinguishable from zero, d about 0.04. The resource model of self-control is not established. What survives is narrower: fatigue changes performance, and motivation and beliefs about willpower modulate it.
p: Do not plan around a willpower budget. Change the cue or the environment instead, and note whether the task still fails.
